national.title: Famed Darth Vader light saber sells for almost $5 million at auction
national.summary: A light saber used by Darth Vader in the "Star Wars" movies "The Empire Strikes Back" and "Return of the Jedi" has sold for nearly $5 million in an auction.
national.body: A light saber used by Darth Vader in the "Star Wars" movies "The Empire Strikes Back" and "Return of the Jedi" sold Thursday for nearly $5 million in an auction. The light saber, which was used in the climactic duel in Cloud City in which Vader tells Luke Skywalker "I am your father" sold for $4.875 million at the Ultimate Star Wars Auction held by Heritage Auctions. The sale marks a world auction record for any "Star Wars" collectible, according to the auction house.The sale also established a new auction record for a screen-used "Star Wars" prop, according to the auction organizer, shooting past its $3.75 million July auction sale of Skywalker's light saber and severed hand-effects rig from "The Empire Strikes Back." Heritage's Thursday auction also featured material from "Star Wars" Episodes I through IX and additional films and TV shows. In addition to Vader's light saber, 27 other "Star Wars" light sabers were assembled for public auction, according to Heritage Auctions.

national.title: Man dies after eating bomb disguised as traditional sweet
national.summary: Some rural communities use the homemade devices to kill wild boars by packing balls of dough with gunpowder, often sourced from firecrackers.
national.body: An Indian man died after a crude bomb disguised as a traditional sweet exploded in his mouth, police said Friday. Some rural communities use the homemade devices to kill wild boars by packing balls of dough with gunpowder, often sourced from firecrackers or quarries. According to the Economic Times, the devices are designed to explode when an animal bites them. But they also resemble a common Indian dessert called rasgulla, a soft, round sweet soaked in sugar syrup -- and traditionally eaten whole. The dead man was identified as 35-year-old Rajendra Barautiya. He was gathered around a bonfire on Tuesday in Dindori district, in the central state of Madhya Pradesh, when a fellow villager brought the "sweet" and another gave it to him. "The bomb, used by some tribal people in the area to kill wild boars, was offered to this man," police officer Rekha Singh told AFP. "It exploded in his mouth." Barautiya was rushed to hospital with severe injuries but died.The villager who handed him the sweet was identified by police as Ramabhagat Barautiya, who described it as a rasgulla, the New Indian Express reported."The incident has triggered widespread shock and fear in the village, with residents struggling to comprehend how a casual evening conversation ended in such a tragic manner," the outlet said.Two men have been arrested and charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder. "We don't know if the motive was to kill, or if it was a mischief," Singh added. "That is a matter of investigation."

national.title: Microsoft battling major worldwide outage
national.summary: A Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted many users, companies and some government operations.
national.body: From Asia to the U.S., a Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted many users, companies and some government operations. Microsoft said early Friday that the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. national.title: Kratom and 7-OH can feel like 'a miracle.' They can also be addictive
national.summary: In the last decade, strong support for kratom and 7-OH products have kept them federally legal. That's started to change. A crackdown for some highly potent products related to kratom is coming.
national.body:
Tyler's opioid addiction began in his early 20s, and when he decided he wanted to quit, he used kratom leaf powders to help ease withdrawal symptoms.

Tyler, now 38, told NPR he thinks kratom helped him stop using opioids for a decade.

Tyler asked NPR to use only his first name because of the stigma attached to his history with drug use and addiction.

Short Wave Kratom and 7-OH products are widely available. They're also at the heart of a public health debate. At first, 7-OH gave him a feeling of euphoria he described as similar to opioids, which "felt like a kind of a miracle," he said.

Nearly a year and a half later, he was in a rapid detox program in Michigan, where he was sedated to sleep through the withdrawals he experienced when he tried to stop taking it.

In the past few years , highly concentrated products with 7-OH — sometimes alongside other semi-synthetic opioids — have popped up online, and at many smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. They can come in the form of tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolate.

7-OH, or 7-hydroxymitragynine, is one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom, which comes from a tree in the coffee family. It's naturally found in kratom in very small amounts, and seems to act more like an opioid in the human brain than kratom leaf products. Kratom is used by some people with opioid addiction to maintain long-term recovery. Some people say it makes them feel energized or focused. Others describe the effects of kratom like those of opioids, and say it can relieve pain, feel calming or even create euphoria.

Some users of 7-OH and kratom show classic signs of addiction, researchers and policy officials say. But the products are not always clearly labeled, so it's difficult or impossible for users to know what quantity of the substances they are consuming.

national.body:
A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products.

Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful.

Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.

Follow live updates: Microsoft scrambles to solve global outage affecting tens of thousands but says fixes not going 'as expected'

What happened? Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".

Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.

Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.

More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.

national.title: FBI recovers $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
national.summary: The FBI says it's seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
national.body: Washington — The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange.The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor.The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total. Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds. Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos. U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program."Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities," First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli said in a Justice Department statement. "Today's seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime."U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro said in the statement that "By springing into action at a moment's notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks. The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets."

national.title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who chastised him
national.summary: Pete Hegseth was yelled at by a sentinel for poor decorum at Arlington National Cemetery. Now the Secretary of Defense has given him a medal.
national.body:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, and his wife Jennifer Rauchet attend a ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on National Veterans Day Observance at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Va., Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption

Coming out of the bruising the Republicans suffered in the midterms, this week was bearing up to be a bad one for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Many thought he'd be the first in the administration to be fired for his support of the Iran war, which proved unpopular with voters.

Then a member of his own party called for a vote to impeach him and, in an embarrassing incident that went viral, he also got chastised for poor decorum when visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

Still, he managed to survive the former – except for Thomas Massie, who sponsored the resolution to impeach him, all other Republicans in the House voted against it – and sought to turn the latter into a PR opportunity.

The day after the impeachment effort, an incident occurred at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, one of America's most sacred military sites. It happened when Hegseth, his wife, and staffers went to lay a wreath at the memorial just outside Washington D.C., to mark Veteran's Day on Wednesday.

Someone in the defense secretary's group laughed loudly, prompting a sentinel on duty at Arlington National Cemetery to shout: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!"

As the video spread on social media, there was a flurry of condemnation online, with some dubbing Hegseth "the secretary of offense."

Political opponents, including Rep. Gwen Moore (D-Wis.), as well as former GOP congressman Adam Kinzinger, criticized Hegseth and his group.

national.title: Rivers in the sky are raining down on the Pacific Northwest. What are they?
national.summary: Atmospheric rivers are large bands of water vapor in the sky. They are dumping trillions of gallons of water on Washington and Oregon, just as high tides and winds batter shorelines.
national.body:
It's the wettest time of the year for one of the wettest parts of the country: the Pacific Northwest.

This week is no exception as heavy rain, high tides and a rising sea level hit the West Coast.

Two atmospheric rivers, bringing heavy rain, will pound parts of Oregon and Washington state back-to-back on Friday and Saturday. Two other atmospheric rivers already dropped multiple inches of rain on both states earlier this week.

Climate Forecasters are predicting a warmer and wetter winter. Here's how El Niño will affect your region "What's really problematic is when you get compounding impacts from multiple atmospheric rivers," said Josh Weiss, a meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Weather Prediction Center. Those impacts include flash flooding, urban flooding and even landslides, he said.

This year's atmospheric river season, which runs from October to March, is off to a fast start, said Weiss.

An atmospheric river is a narrow band of water vapor pushed by the wind. Loaded up with moisture, it dumps rain or snow. These rivers can be up to 2,000 miles long and 600 miles wide, said F. Martin Ralph, the director of the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

"It's literally a river in the sky," said Ralph, one of the leading researchers on atmospheric rivers. These rivers are a natural climate pattern. In fact, about 50 to 60% of rain in California comes from atmospheric rivers, Weiss said.

national.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
national.summary: The forthcoming move has left some parents and educators frustrated and wondering about the company's motivations.
national.body:
If schools don't want Google AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Don Ryan/AP/AP hide caption

Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.

An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.

"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."

Mental Health Nearly 2 out of 3 teens and tweens use AI chatbots, new research shows When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens , first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom .

But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified , Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.

In a post on X , New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.

Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.

national.title: Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients
national.summary: Republicans and Democrats in North Dakota worked together to limit what people with diabetes have to pay for insulin, joining a growing bipartisan push across the country to protect patients.
national.body:
HILLSBORO, N.D. — The Kritzberger family has farmed in the Red River Valley for more than a century. They once had livestock. Now they grow sugar beets, soybeans and grains.

Health Reporting in the States Republicans and Democrats find a unifying target: Pharmacy benefit managers "We're in an incredible amount of debt," Ang Kritzberger said as she walked the farm on a recent fall morning.

For the past 10 years, the Kritzbergers have had another worry. Their daughter Nina has Type 1 diabetes. That landed the family in a national debate about how to protect patients from high insulin costs.

"I slept by her bedside for the first 60 days," Ang Kritzberger said. "And I had to stick her finger every two hours, 24 hours a day, to make sure that she was OK."

Ang Kritzberger with daughter Nina, who has Type 1 diabetes. Nina's condition​​ landed the family in a national debate about how to protect patients from high insulin costs. Hannah Norman/KFF Health News hide caption

The Kritzbergers also pay a lot out-of-pocket every year for medical care, despite having insurance — at least $8,000 for drugs, supplies and medical appointments.

That's not uncommon. Soaring insulin prices for years forced people with diabetes to pay hundreds, even thousands, of dollars. Many rationed insulin, with sometimes deadly consequences.

But today, there's a growing movement across the country to cap what people with diabetes pay for insulin. That's brought together Democrats and Republicans, tapping an emerging consensus that the government should protect people from high drug prices.

national.title: Why even a fraction of a degree can escalate climate change impacts
national.summary: Countries are not meeting their goal of limiting climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius. How much hotter the planet gets makes a profound difference for the impacts the world could see.
national.body:
Countries have gathered at the annual climate change negotiations at the COP31 summit in Turkey to discuss how to achieve a goal that is increasingly unachievable. A decade ago, countries agreed to limit climate warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit). Now, that goal is out of reach.

Globally, average temperatures are already close to 1.5 degrees Celsius warmer than they were before the Industrial Revolution. Heat-trapping emissions from burning fossil fuels are still rising in the atmosphere, and most countries are not on track to meet their climate pledges to cut emissions by transitioning to cleaner energy.

The best-case scenario for the planet is now 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius of warming (roughly 3 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a recent United Nations study . If fossil fuel emissions stay on their current path, the world would be around 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter by the end of the century.

While the difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees Celsius may seem tiny, scientific research shows those increments can produce dramatically different outcomes for the planet. More warming raises the risk of extreme weather globally and could lead to the collapse of some of the planet's most sensitive ecosystems.

"The crucial point is that every fraction of a degree matters," says Tim Lenton, climate professor at the University of Exeter. "Every fraction of a degree that we avoid is really able to do a huge amount of limiting harm."

Corals are architects of an entire ecosystem. As they grow, they create the framework that supports vast numbers of other species, making reefs biodiversity hotspots. They're also vital to hundreds of millions of people who depend on them for food and livelihoods.

Climate Some of the most pristine coral reefs have a secret weapon: birds Corals are also highly vulnerable to heat. Prolonged marine heat waves cause corals to bleach, turning them white, which can eventually kill corals. Since the late 1990s, there have been four global bleaching events. With a historically strong El Niño now raising water temperatures, scientists say the fifth global bleaching event is likely unfolding.

Even before the previous bleaching event from 2023 to 2025, researchers found that 44% of coral species globally are at risk of extinction.

national.title: The cost of college is confusing. Some schools are trying to change that
national.summary: Many Americans have soured on higher education because of how frustratingly hard it is to figure out what they will pay to attend.
national.body:
An aerial view of the Middlebury College campus in Vermont. Middlebury is among a number of colleges trying to help people decipher how much they actually cost, by guaranteeing free tuition for families with incomes under a particular threshold. Oliver Parini for The Hechinger Report hide caption

MIDDLEBURY, Vt. — Stately buildings of Vermont limestone surround meticulously tended lawns in a village that could be the setting for a Hallmark Christmas movie.

Middlebury College looks … expensive. But like other universities and colleges, it's working hard to persuade people that it's not.

Middlebury has announced that students from families with household incomes up to $175,000 can enroll tuition-free . That makes it one of a growing number of colleges trying to reduce widespread public confusion about what college actually costs.

These offers may seem like generous expansions of financial aid; after all, $175,000 is more than double the nation's median household income .

Cost of Living College 'sticker prices' have risen dramatically. Here's why But while it's true that a few additional families will benefit — 35 to 50 in the incoming class at Middlebury, which typically enrolls about 630 new students per year, the college says — most people from families earning $175,000 or less already attend without having to pay tuition.

The real purpose of what Middlebury and other schools are doing, experts say, is to confront a problem that has soured many Americans on higher education: how frustratingly hard it is to figure out what college will cost.

"Let's make it as non-complicated as possible," said Ian Baucom, president at Middlebury: "If your family income is $175,000 or less, at Middlebury, you don't pay tuition." What the school is doing, he said, is trying to "just [be] really clear and get that out of the way, and then let the students decide."

national.title: These two voter turnout trends explain what happened across the South in the election
national.summary: In six states across the Deep South, a drastic swing to the left this election was driven by high Black voter turnout and compounded by a sharp decline in voting rates across Republican-heavy areas.
national.body:
Democratic victories in the South this year were driven just as much by who showed up to vote as who stayed home, according to an NPR analysis of turnout data.

Midterm elections normally have lower voter participation than presidential contests. But from Louisiana to the Carolinas, counties that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 came closer to matching — and in some cases exceeding — presidential turnout. At the same time, counties won by President Trump saw a much sharper decline in turnout and fewer Republican votes.

In six southern states — Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina — turnout dropped by 19% in Harris-won counties compared to 26% in Trump-won counties. (In Louisiana, counties are called parishes).

Only on NPR The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election Across the South, the six states analyzed swung an average of 22 points towards Democrats, larger than the national swing of about 14.5 points.

This differential turnout was a key factor in Democrats flipping Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Mississippi, and contributed to the closer-than-expected margin in Louisiana's Senate race.

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom outperformed Harris, earning roughly 8,100 more votes than she did in 2024. Colom's margin over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is just over 5,600 votes as final ballots are being tallied.

Democratic Senate nominees in those six states earned more raw votes than Harris in 170 counties. On the flip side, the Republican nominees garnered hundreds of thousands fewer votes than Trump.

In special elections and primaries leading up to the midterms, voting data and polls showed a surge in Black voter participation, spurred in part by a Supreme Court decision that gutted part of the Voting Rights Act.

Democratic victories in the South this year were driven just as much by who showed up to vote as who stayed home, according to an NPR analysis of turnout data.

Midterm elections normally have lower voter participation than presidential contests. But from Louisiana to the Carolinas, counties that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 came closer to matching — and in some cases exceeding — presidential turnout. At the same time, counties won by President Trump saw a much sharper decline in turnout and fewer Republican votes.

In six southern states — Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina — turnout dropped by 19% in Harris-won counties compared to 26% in Trump-won counties. (In Louisiana, counties are called parishes).

Only on NPR The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election Across the South, the six states analyzed swung an average of 22 points towards Democrats, larger than the national swing of about 14.5 points.

This differential turnout was a key factor in Democrats flipping Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Mississippi, and contributed to the closer-than-expected margin in Louisiana's Senate race.

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom outperformed Harris, earning roughly 8,100 more votes than she did in 2024. Colom's margin over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is just over 5,600 votes as final ballots are being tallied.

Democratic Senate nominees in those six states earned more raw votes than Harris in 170 counties. On the flip side, the Republican nominees garnered hundreds of thousands fewer votes than Trump.

In special elections and primaries leading up to the midterms, voting data and polls showed a surge in Black voter participation, spurred in part by a Supreme Court decision that gutted part of the Voting Rights Act.

national.title: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
national.summary: Claims the entire Australian team knew of the 2018 sandpaper cheating plot are dividing the cricket world.
national.body:
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.

Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.

"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."

A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.

Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."

national.body:
Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.

Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.

"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.

Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.

Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.

"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.

Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.

The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.

national.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
national.summary: Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs.
national.body:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.

Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.

Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.

Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.

national.summary: Van Hollen, a progressive from Maryland, said voters sent a clear message in the midterm elections — that they want "change from the status quo."
national.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has announced he will challenge New York's Chuck Schumer for the job of Senate majority leader, pushing the party into a fresh debate over its future just days after sweeping victories in the midterm elections.

Van Hollen made the announcement on Thursday, saying voters sent a clear message in the midterms — that they want "change from the status quo."

"It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said in a statement. "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

Congress House GOP elects Jim Jordan as new leader as the party looks to rebuild from midterms Van Hollen, 67, was elected to the Senate in 2016 after spending more than a decade in the House representing a Maryland suburb outside of Washington, D.C. One of his party's more progressive members, he gained national attention last year lobbying for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia after he was wrongfully deported to a prison in El Salvador.

His announcement comes at a moment when progressive activists, as well as some Democratic lawmakers, are calling for Schumer, 75, to be replaced as party leader. Schumer has served in the role since 2017, but drew the ire of many inside the Democratic base for not taking a tougher stance against President Trump during a fight over government funding in early 2025.

"I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I'm proud of what we've accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer wrote on social media following Van Hollen's announcement. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."

While Schumer has maintained he has the votes to become majority leader, he has faced growing resistance from inside the Democratic caucus. Earlier this week, Sen. Bernie Sanders, the Vermont Independent who aligns with Democrats, said he would oppose Schumer. He made the announcement next to Michigan Democrat Elissa Slotkin, who did not say outright she would oppose Schumer, but told reporters, "I am seeking change."

Several incoming Democratic lawmakers have similarly expressed opposition to Schumer's bid for majority leader, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, described a harrowing scene, saying workers "who had only barely survived themselves turned back and dug victims out of the rubble".

The city's fire commissioner, Lillian Bonsignore, said firefighters were on the scene within minutes and called their actions "incredibly heroic".

Rescue operations ended about 24 hours later on Thursday after fire officials determined there were no more victims at the site.

The site has now been turned over to the Department of Buildings and the New York police.

national.title: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
national.summary: More than 900 victims are thought to have fallen prey to the FaceStealer scheme in the last 18 months.
national.body:
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.

More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.

This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.

US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.

Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.

Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.

national.title: 'How does a building just fall?' Neighbours grieve after deadly Brooklyn building collapse
national.summary: The accident rattled the usually calm immigrant neighbourhood of Flatbush, New York. At least eight residents, including two children, died in the rubble.
national.body:
Over the loud noise of her radio, Ann Marie did not hear the sound of the Brooklyn building behind her home collapse on Wednesday night, but she soon saw the flashing lights of fire department trucks rushing to the scene.

When she made her way out to the wreckage, workers were still searching for bodies. One of the building's walls had torn off, exposing the inside of several apartment homes, and the rubble had collapsed into a construction site next door.

At least eight of her neighbours died in the accident - six adults and two children, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. Five of the victims were residents, CBS reported.

"Right now, I'm really scared," Marie told the BBC. "Now that I'm seeing exactly this side of the building, you can imagine the fright of those people, what happened to them."

On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani said he had visited survivors in hospital. Eighteen people were injured, including four firefighters. One person is in critical condition.

"I want to take a moment to remember those we have so senselessly lost," Mamdani added. "These were our friends and our neighbours, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Trinidad and beyond."

national.body:
A doctor who had been in an ongoing dispute over mould and other issues at his Washington DC apartment fatally shot his building's manager and fired at four others before killing himself, police say.

Building manager James Stuart, 46, was pronounced dead at the scene, while four others were rushed to local hospitals for treatment.

The shooting began on Thursday morning local time inside a gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle neighbourhood, which is about a mile (1.6km) north of the White House.

Police said the suspect, identified as 55-year-old doctor Matt Wade Lambert, then barricaded himself in an apartment, and later died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

While the suspect was barricaded, "he did fire through the door at officers at least on two occasions", Jefferey Carroll, the interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, said at a news conference.

Negotiators had been on the phone with the suspect when they heard a gunshot and he stopped communicating with them, according to Carroll.

Officers forced their way into the apartment and saw the suspect had what appeared to be a "self-inflicted gunshot wound", he said.

Authorities are still working to understand the exact timeline, suspect's motivation, and other details of the incident.

European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.

Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.

The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.

But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but there were no further details over how many prisoners would be exchanged or when it would happen.

national.title: Senators probe RFK Jr.'s reason for Samoa trip after letter refuting his testimony published
national.summary: Two Democratic senators are launching an investigation into whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress about his reason for a 2019 trip to Samoa after The Associated Press and The Guardian published documents in August refuting his testimony.
national.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Two Democratic senators are launching an investigation into whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress about his reason for a 2019 trip to Samoa after The Associated Press and The Guardian published documents in August refuting his testimony.

AP and Guardian reporting in August showed that while Kennedy repeatedly told senators who held the key to his confirmation last year that his visit to Samoa before a deadly measles outbreak had "nothing to do with vaccines," a letter he sent to the Samoan prime minister ahead of the trip showed otherwise. In the letter, Kennedy used the words vaccine or vaccination eight times.

The new inquiry is one of a vast array of investigations planned into the Trump administration after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate from Republicans in the midterm elections.

Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., said in a letter Wednesday to Children's Health Defense, a nonprofit group known for anti-vaccine activism that was formerly chaired by Kennedy, that they were starting an investigation.

The lawmakers asked the group for a broad range of documents related to Kennedy's Samoa travel, his 2024 presidential campaign and his Senate confirmation process. The letter also requested all communications between the group and federal government officials since President Donald Trump's second term began in January 2025. The senators gave the group a deadline of Dec. 4 to comply.

"We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children," Wyden and Alsobrooks wrote in their letter. "We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate's ability to fulfill its constitutional duties."

The Department of Health and Human Services has maintained that the Samoa visit "was unrelated to vaccines." In response to an AP inquiry in August, it said "any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory."

Kennedy was not under oath during his confirmation hearing. Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence regardless of whether a person is under oath, though it is rarely prosecuted.

national.title: Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state
national.summary: Alaskans are still waiting for the full results, including in the close Senate race between Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.
national.body:
For the last few weeks, in addition to its usual payload of passengers, medicine, and supplies, Alaska Seaplanes has carried some unique cargo: midterm election ballots.

The regional airline is a piece of a complex logistical puzzle that sees Alaskans' ballots cast by mail and in person carried across the vast expanse of America's largest state, which is primarily connected by water and air rather than roads.

This considerable task explains why, a week after most US states knew their results in the midterms - in which the Democrats won back both chambers of Congress from the Republicans - Alaskans are still waiting for the Senate race to be called.

The victor in this close contest between the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, former congresswoman Mary Peltola, could remain unknown until 18 November, when officials expect to have counted all eligible ballots.

"We do feel a sense of pride of making sure we do the job right - the really complicated job of getting all these ballots across thousands of miles in Alaska," Andy Kline, the marketing director of Alaska Seaplanes, which serves the south-eastern part of the state, told the BBC.

"We feel like we're part of the last leg of that journey of those ballots."

Some precincts in Alaska are able to communicate their initial results to centralised election offices on election night, allowing state officials and news outlets to report some preliminary vote tallies.

But it takes some time for the full picture of how people have voted to emerge.

national.title: What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports more than 500 cases this year
national.summary: As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself.
national.body:
On Nov. 5, low flying helicopters blanketed areas of Florida's Pinellas and Hillsborough counties with a fine mist. It's one of the ways Florida health officials hope to slow the country's largest dengue fever outbreak in more than a decade.

Dengue starts with a mosquito bite, so killing the insects is key. The helicopters spray water mixed with Bti , a natural bacteria found in soil that kills black fly and mosquito larvae.

Most people become infected when traveling in high dengue risk areas, and Florida had recorded 382 international travel-associated cases as of Oct. 31. But the state has also counted a recent record high number of people infected on Florida's turf: 524 .

Florida has had domestic dengue outbreaks before. In 2010, it counted 58 locally acquired cases, after nearly eight decades of reprieve . Since then, the largest outbreak was in 2023, when the state reported 189 dengue cases contracted in Florida.

As Florida navigates its largest dengue outbreak in more than 15 years, it might help to understand how this virus spreads and how to recognize symptoms and protect yourself. We sought answers to some pressing dengue fever questions.

Dengue fever can develop after a person is infected with any of the four dengue viruses . The virus is not transmitted person-to-person , and there is no widely available vaccine to prevent infection.

About 3 in 4 people do not get sick, but if symptoms develop, they typically set in about four to 10 days after an infected mosquito's bite.

The most common symptoms of mild dengue fever include high fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, pain behind the eyes and muscle, joint and bone pain.

local.summary: After 45 years as the artistic director for Borinquen Dance Theatre, its founder Nydia Padilla-Rodriguez is retiring in December.

Growing up in Rochester, dancing wasn't encouraged in his home, Bermudez said. But after getting into trouble at Monroe Middle School, staff member and mentor Sandra Martinez insisted he stay after school for a program that would change his life.

Decades later, Bermudez is preparing to take the reins of Borinquen Dance Theatre , succeeding founder Nydia Padilla-Rodriguez, who is retiring in December after 45 years as the organization's artistic director. In that time, she built an award-winning, youth-oriented program aimed at building self-confidence and discipline through dance while celebrating Puerto Rican culture.

For Bermudez, the new role represents a new chapter in a career shaped by dance, mentorship, and a commitment to helping the youth.

Bermudez was born in Puerto Rico but mainly grew up in the city of Rochester.

He described himself as an at-risk youth and was very angry at the family dynamics he experienced at home.

He said dancing wasn't considered masculine in his household. Martinez sent a letter to his parents saying he was staying after school for extra help when in reality he was joining a dance program, which Bermudez ended up loving.

"I got into some trouble and Sandra (Martinez) was the one that said, "You're going to stay after school for a program,’ and I said, ‘No, I'm not.’ She said, ‘Yes, you are.’ It was a dance program. I said, ‘No, I'm not.’” Bermudez said.

Years later, Bermudez became a part of the Movida Dance Company in Rochester, where he taught and performed as a principal dancer for 15 years. It was during his time at Movida where he was exposed to Borinquen Dance Theatre at its performances. The two companies shared a dance studio at the time.

local.body:
James Richard Morrison (Jim), age 76, passed away on November 11th, 2026 at home with his family beside him, Jim leaves behind a lifetime of memories and a family who loved him dearly.

Jim was a hard worker. He spent many years on the road as an over-the-road truck driver, later driving for Hope's Windows, and eventually working for Lakeshore Septic. Jim was never one to sit idle. There was always something to do, something to fix, or someone to share a joke with. He always had a story to tell and was quick with his famous Dad-joke wit.

For many years, Jim enjoyed hunting and fishing, a love he happily passed along to his children and grandchildren. He found enjoyment in the simple things: tinkering in the garage, collecting his John Deere tractors, puttering with his apple press, and working with his honey bees. Sitting on the front porch relaxing, or just enjoying time with his devoted dog Macie, who never left his side. He also enjoyed sharing his knowledge with anyone willing to spend a little time with him. Jim was always ready to teach someone something new. Like building Butterfly houses.

Jim knew the value of a dollar and made sure to pass that lesson along to his children. He believed in hard work and solid values. Whether it was pulling nails to recycle or saving things to repurpose, Jim never believed in letting anything go to waste. He could find a use for just about anything. But while he was careful with a dollar, he was never cheap when it came to the people he loved. He made sure his family never went without, and if he knew someone was in need, Jim would be the first to lend a hand, helping however he could and giving the shirt off his back if necessary. That was just the kind of man he was.

But above all, Jim's greatest joy was his family. He treasured the everyday moments and the life he built with his wife. He was a devoted husband of almost 52 years to his cherished wife, Priscilla (Frazier). Her "Jimmy" was the love of her life. You rarely saw one without the other.

He was a loving father to his daughter, Stephanie (Steven) Horner of Cherry Creek, and his son, James (Cassandra) Morrison of Randolph. He was a proud and loving grandfather to his four grandsons, Ethan (Bubba), Finnley, Grayson, and Henry, who meant the world to him. Being a Grandpa changed Jim, his kids often joked how much the grandkids got away with what "we never would have!" He truly loved his boys and sharing his knowledge of things with them.

local.title: Fredonia eyes bond note for water project
local.summary: Three Fredonia trustees devoted their board meeting reports this week to the water system saga. Most notably, Trustee Tim Mulholland said the village is eyeing a bond anticipation note to help fund its North County Water District connection project. Mulholland described a meeting about financing opt
local.body:
Three Fredonia trustees devoted their board meeting reports this week to the water system saga.

Most notably, Trustee Tim Mulholland said the village is eyeing a bond anticipation note to help fund its North County Water District connection project.

Mulholland described a meeting about financing options for the project. Financial consultant Rick Ganci, Trustee LeeAnn Lazarony, and Treasurer Erlyssa LeBsau joined him in the meeting.

The Fredonia officials gave Ganci a "financial snapshot of our village. One of the immediate priorities is reimbursing our village’s water fund for approximately $500,000 in engineering and related project expenses already incurred before our recent pause."

Mulholland continued, "We discussed whether it would make more sense to pursue financing for the entire project, or focus initially on reimbursing the water fund. Given that the project’s ultimate financing needs are still being determined, that we anticipate potential grant funding, and we aren't ready to move forward with this project during this pause, the appropriate approach appears to be to pay back our water fund as an appropriate first step, and Ganci agreed."

LeBeau consulted with Ganci to confirm that a September resolution provides sufficient authorization to do a bond anticipation note, Mulholland said. "This short term borrowing mechanism will allow us to reimburse the water fund for those expenses already paid," he said.

Ganci wants to have the note ready by December, and "also offered to have his team review the project’s finances, and other potential funding opportunities and grants that may be available to us," Mulholland added.

"While municipalities our size have limited options, it is worth exploring opportunities to strengthen our finances without unnecessarily burdening our taxpayers. That's very important to all of us, and myself, especially," he concluded.

local.title: Are Democrats serious about affordability?
local.summary: Emboldened by the scale of Democratic victories in the midterms, a small group of liberals is trying to blow up a carefully negotiated bipartisan agreement that would make it easier to build in America. Failure to pass this compromise during the lame-duck session would send a loud message that the i
local.body:
Emboldened by the scale of Democratic victories in the midterms, a small group of liberals is trying to blow up a carefully negotiated bipartisan agreement that would make it easier to build in America. Failure to pass this compromise during the lame-duck session would send a loud message that the incoming Democratic majorities aren't as serious about affordability as candidates said they were on the stump. And a deal this good for the economy is unlikely to materialize in the next Congress, which is why unions for the building trades and electricians are fighting to get it done.

Unfortunately, Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), the presumptive next House speaker, wants to reopen negotiations. His spokesperson said on Thursday that the deal "falls short in several areas." Without expressing opposition, Jeffries's office said: "We must once again support the clean energy economy and combat the climate crisis with the fierce urgency of now."

Except the deal on the table is great for the environment. Democratic negotiators in the Senate consulted closely with their House counterparts. The agreement would make it much easier to build clean energy projects and the transmission lines needed to connect them to the grid. While some environmental groups criticize the compromise for reducing regulatory barriers to construct fossil fuel infrastructure, a recent analysis by the independent Rhodium Group concluded that the legislation would probably cut carbon emissions overall.

Given the soaring demand for energy, the reforms are necessary to boost production capacity and thereby lower electricity prices for Americans. The Rhodium analysis projects that if the bill passes, the average household would see its electricity bills drop $50 to $78 a year by 2040. The legislation also includes a provision obligating states to require large energy consumers, such as data centers, to pay for their electricity use.

Unfortunately, there is a potent "degrowth" faction inside the environmental movement for whom no deal would ever be good enough. These activists don't want to create enough supply to meet energy needs. They want to make it harder to build, in the hope that scarcity will force society to reduce consumption. Down that path lies national stagnation.

Other Democrats may want an agreement but see an opening to maximize leverage. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-California), poised to lead the House committee that oversees permitting reform, has argued for weeks that Democrats should hold out until next year to negotiate more favorable terms.

local.title: Longtime Steelers assistant coach Dick Hoak dies at 86
local.summary: PITTSBURGH (AP) — Dick Hoak, who spent more than 45 years with the Pittsburgh Steelers as a player and then an assistant coach, winning five Super Bowl rings along the way, has died. He was 86. The team announced Hoak’s death on Wednesday. No cause of death was given. “Dick represented everything th
local.body:
PITTSBURGH (AP) -- Dick Hoak, who spent more than 45 years with the Pittsburgh Steelers as a player and then an assistant coach, winning five Super Bowl rings along the way, has died. He was 86.

The team announced Hoak’s death on Wednesday. No cause of death was given.

“Dick represented everything the Steelers stand for with his toughness, loyalty, dedication and an unwavering commitment to the team,” team president Art Rooney II said in a statement.

Selected by the Steelers in the seventh round of the 1961 NFL draft after a standout career at Penn State, Hoak ran for 3,965 yards and 25 touchdowns in 10 seasons in Pittsburgh’s backfield, leading the then-struggling club in rushing three times.

Hoak, a Pro Bowler in 1968 after running for a career-best 858 yards, retired after the 1970 season and joined coach Chuck Noll’s staff as running backs coach in 1972.

Over the next three-plus decades, he served as an important touchstone and mentor for future Hall of Famers like Franco Harris and Jerome Bettis as the Steelers evolved from also-rans to one of the league’s marquee franchises.

Many of those Super Bowl-winning teams were powered by the running game that Hoak helped mold. He was so influential and important to the organization that he spanned the tenure of a pair of Hall of Fame coaches in Noll and his successor, Bill Cowher.

Cowher retained Hoak on his staff after replacing Noll in 1992 and credited Hoak for helping him shoulder the difficult task of replacing an icon.

local.body:
ASHVILLE -- A final informational forum for the Clymer, Sherman and Panama school district communities is set for the end of this month, giving residents one more chance to ask questions and get more information before the final statutory vote is scheduled.

The meeting is set to take place at 6:30 p.m. at the Ashville Hewes BOCES on November 30. The meeting is open to all community members and will be recorded and uploaded to the CSPHub website for anyone unable to attend.

"We will highlight the final recommendations from the independent feasibility study," CSP Merger Study Project Coordinator, Shelly O'Boyle, said. "Additionally, White and Partners will present updated financial data. A major focus of the format is giving residents a dedicated platform to ask questions and discuss the findings."

The town hall is the final public forum before the formal statutory vote, which is the vote that officially decides if the three districts will merge. O'Boyle said the vote has been scheduled by the New York State Commissioner of Education.

The official date for the statutory vote is December 15 from 12 p.m. to 8 p.m. Absentee ballots will be available starting on November 12.

"Voting will take place locally at each individual school district," O'Boyle said. "Residents will be able to obtain absentee and early mail ballots from their respective District Clerks. Military voters should request an early mail ballot. Proof of residency should be brought to the voting site."

The full merger feasibility study, past meetings, and more information on the CSP merger can be found at CSPHub.org.

local.title: Alvarez, PCA win unanimous MVPs
local.summary: Pete Crow-Armstrong won the NL MVP award unanimously on Thursday after the center fielder starred for the Chicago Cubs in a majestic all-around season. Crow-Armstrong joined Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez as first-time MVPs. Alvarez was the unanimous AL winner after making a run at the Triple
local.body:
Pete Crow-Armstrong won the NL MVP award unanimously on Thursday after the center fielder starred for the Chicago Cubs in a majestic all-around season.

Crow-Armstrong joined Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez as first-time MVPs. Alvarez was the unanimous AL winner after making a run at the Triple Crown, hitting a career-high .316 with 42 homers and 106 RBIs for the AL West champions.

Crow-Armstrong set career highs by batting .280 with 45 homers, 107 RBIs and 41 steals in 162 games. He tied Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead in home runs, and he led the NL in runs (119), slugging percentage (.570) and OPS (.942).

He also was one of the majors’ premier defensive players. The Southern California native won his second Gold Glove, and he led the majors with 26 Outs Above Average and 23 Runs Prevented, according to Baseball Savant.

“You spend your whole life in baseball and you just don’t see this happen on a baseball field,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said after Crow-Armstrong homered twice in an 8-4 win over Atlanta on Sept. 16. “You’re grateful to be a part of it. You’re grateful to see things like this and then you’re grateful that the fans get to see a season like this.”

Crow-Armstrong received all 30 first-place votes in balloting from the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. Four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers finished second, and Milwaukee Brewers second baseman Brice Turang was third.

Alvarez led the majors in batting average and finished in a tie for second in the AL in homers and second by himself in RBIs, trailing Pete Alonso’s 43 homers and 113 RBIs for Baltimore.

Alvarez was Houston’s primary designated hitter, but his offensive brilliance was enough to overcome his limited contributions on defense. The four-time All-Star also led the majors in walks (109), on-base percentage (.432) and slugging percentage (.601).

The Bears senior guard completed her celebratory signing letter Thursday afternoon to atte
local.body:
Playing high-level college basketball has always been a dream for Jadyn Trocki.

When the closest Division I program to her Frewsburg home came calling a couple of years ago, it felt like the perfect situation.

The Bears senior guard completed her celebratory signing letter Thursday afternoon to attend St. Bonaventure University and play basketball for the Bonnies beginning next fall.

"Division I has always been the dream, but some DIIs were also in the equation as well," Trocki said Wednesday afternoon. "I wasn't always set on DI. I was always going to choose where I fit best."

Trocki has put together the best individual career in Frewsburg history and with it the Bears have also experienced high levels of success as a team. She is already Frewsburg's all-time leading scorer with 1,796 points and has been named the New York State Sportswriters Association's Class C Player of the Year in back-to-back seasons.

"A lot of people focus on the skill side of things, but I remember on jayvee she would get really emotional, so for me the fun part has been seeing her mental maturity. Even from the beginning of last season to the end, or during her sophomore year, she would go into a shell," Frewsburg head coach Sierra Beaver said Wednesday. "Last year, I think one of the first things I noticed at North Tonawanda was that things weren't going well in the first half and I remember at halftime, telling Sandy (Ruhlman, Jadyn's mother) we'll see how the season goes based on this second half. If Jadyn goes into a shell we're in trouble, but if she shows maturity, we're going to have a fun season. In the second half she had one of her best games."

Trocki has started every year since eighth grade after being called up to the varsity team for a postseason run at the end of her seventh-grade year.

"Around seventh grade I started taking it more seriously," Trocki said. "I started playing for bigger programs, playing throughout Pittsburgh and Erie. ... It's the one thing I really love."

local.title: Holland Willows hosting annual food drive to benefit Colden Food Pantry
local.summary: Family-owned Holland Willows is hosting its second annual food drive on Saturday, with proceeds benefiting the Bread of Life Outreach Center in Colden.
local.body: As food pantries face increased demand heading into the holiday season, one longtime Southtowns business is hoping to make a difference by bringing the community together.Family-owned Holland Willows is hosting its second annual food drive on Saturday, with proceeds benefiting the Bread of Life Outreach Center in Colden.The drive runs 7 to 10 p.m., and features live music from the Whiskey River Band, along with food and drink specials, giveaways and a 50/50 raffle. Organizers are encouraging people to bring canned goods and other nonperishable food items.For more than five decades, Holland Willows has been a gathering place for the Southtowns community. Organizers said the food drive is another way to give back to the people who have supported the business over the years."We decided it's time to do something, do a food drive, especially during this time when people are in need," Kimberly Brisky said. Brisky is a member of the band and one of the event's organizers.Brisky said this year's event is expected to be even bigger, with proceeds going directly to the Colden Food Pantry.WATCH: Holland Willows hosting annual food drive to benefit Colden Food PantryCheryl Shene, who is also helping organize the drive, said the community response was incredible during its inaugural year.Organizers said supporting resources is especially important in rural communities, where residents may not always have the same access to assistance.The Bread of Life Outreach Center operates through donations and provides food assistance to people in need.Those who cannot attend Saturday's event can still contribute. Food donations will also be accepted at Holland Willows during regular business hours through November 14.Organizers hope the event will not only stock the pantry's shelves but also remind people of the impact a community can have when it comes together to support its neighbors.

local.title: New Allentown bar to pay homage to The Old Pink
local.summary: A new dive bar is set to open in Buffalo's Allentown and will pay homage to The Old Pink through late nights, music and a one-sandwich menu.
local.body: A new dive bar is set to open in Buffalo's Allentown and will pay homage to The Old Pink through late nights, music and a one-sandwich menu.The bar, Damaged Goods, is named after a song by the post-punk band Gang of Four. It is the latest from Mike Shatzel, a seasoned veteran of Buffalo's bar and restaurant industry. Shatzel's the owner of multiple establishments, including Cole's on Elmwood, Colter Bay and The Terrace in Delaware Park. "I've been all over the world and The Old Pink was my favorite bar I've ever been to," Shatzel said. The new bar will revitalize Shatzel's previous business at 175 Allen Street, Allentown Burger Venture, which closed in February. He said the new business will be "a new wave punk rock dive bar," aiming to open by Thanksgiving. WATCH: New Allentown bar to pay homage to The Old PinkShatzel's hoping to revitalize some nightlife lost in the neighborhood after The Old Pink and Mulligan's Brick Bar were lost to fires within a year of each other. While Shatzel tells me it's impossible to replace The Old Pink, people will find a few nods to the legendary bar at Damaged Goods. "Definitely the music," Shatzel said. "Eric, the old DJ from The Pink, will be here a couple of nights a week."The Pink's 4 a.m. closing time was a draw for some, and Shatzel told me he's hoping to stay open until around 3 a.m. on weekends. And perhaps most importantly, will there be a steak sandwich on offer?"Steak sandwich I think will run occasionally," Shatzel said. "Right now, we're gonna be doing a shaved prime rib sandwich. Just one sandwich, that's it."But along with the gaps left by fires, vacant storefronts also show signs of strain on businesses along Allen Street. Shatzel said it hasn't been the same since the Covid-19 pandemic, but he's betting on the bar and new wave/post-punk music crowd for his latest venture."I think the kids, they'll catch on if there's a good vibe," Shatzel said. "They're gonna wanna enjoy it as well."

local.title: Where's the school bus? No regular afternoon bus this week for a West Buffalo Charter 8th grader
local.summary: For the third time this week, Jaime Hodge says her eighth-grade son won't have a bus to take him home from West Buffalo Charter after school.
local.body: For the third time this week, Jaime Hodge says her eighth-grade son won't have a bus to take him home from West Buffalo Charter after school.On Monday and Tuesday, Hodge and her husband took turns picking him up. On Thursday, the school sent a pre-recorded call offering a bus ride an hour earlier than when school lets out."Unfortunately, the bus contacted us to let us know a driver is unavailable again for bus 458 today," the message said. "After working with them to find a solution, they've offered to send a bus at 2 p.m." Hodge said this is an important time in her son Zander's academic career as he prepares for high school and college. "Him missing any type of classes, especially math because he wants to go into engineering, is very detrimental to his future education," Hodge said.Hodge said she's been dealing with spotty transportation for her son since Kindergarten. Buffalo Public Schools provide transportation to West Buffalo Charter through a contract with transportation company, First Student. "With the Buffalo Public Schools already in such a deficit for funding, I would think they would want to relook at the contract but actually hold First Student to the lines in that contract. Because they aren't fulfilling what we're paying them for." WATCH: Where's the school bus? No regular afternoon bus this week for a West Buffalo Charter 8th graderI reached out to Buffalo Public Schools and First Student.A Buffalo Schools spokesman said in a statement that "as a result of these concerns, the district will reach out to First Student directly." They urged parents to keep track of their children's buses through the First Student app but to call directly to seek assistance at (716) 816-4895.They also acknowledged that there's a national bus driver shortage and First Student is actively recruiting drivers.

local.title: 'I didn't know what to do': Clergy abuse survivor shares his story
local.summary: A clergy abuse survivor reached out to share their story as the Catholic Diocese of Buffalo gets closer to settling nearly 900 Child Victims Act cases.
local.body: A clergy abuse survivor reached out to share their story as the Catholic Diocese of Buffalo gets closer to settling nearly 900 Child Victims Act cases."I've suffered for years with this in my head," Gregg Siddons said.Siddons, a Western New York native, now lives in Erie, Pennsylvania. He tells me he lives with post-traumatic stress and daily nightmares of what happened to him as a teenager."The physical abuse that was done to me and the sexual abuse and how this priest took advantage of me and there was nothing I could do," Siddons said. Siddons said in a week he'll be turning 67, but for the last 53 years of his life, he has been tormented by the memory of being molested by a Roman Catholic priest when he was only 14 years of age.It happened to him at Saints Peter and Paul Church in Williamsville. The priest was Monsignor George Zimphfer.Siddons tells me, as a troubled teen, his parents sent him to live at the then Gateway Methodist youth home, not far from the church. That's when he started to attend in 1973, where he said his accuser abused him multiple times."I thought going was gonna help me, and then I met a Catholic priest that I thought was gonna be my friend and be able to talk to, and he just took advantage of me, and I was extremely naive," Siddons said. "I didn't know what to do. I didn't know who to talk to, what to say. I remember every time." WATCH: 'I didn't know what to do': Clergy abuse survivor shares his storySiddons tells me he tried to tell his counselors and his parents, but no one believed him."'A priest is not gonna do this to you.' I tried to tell my parents. No one wanted to believe us," Siddons stated. "I grew up in the 60s, and no one believed children. They looked at children as if we're all liars."He's now one of the hundreds of Child Victims Act cases filed against the Diocese of Buffalo.Siddons tells me he has voted in favor of the $327 million settlement being decided, but he said no money will ever take his pain away.WATCH: Buffalo Diocese clergy abuse survivors to receive $327 million"Nightmares daily. I see a psychiatrist once a month. I take medication. I'm also epileptic. I have seizures," Siddons said. local.title: Niagara Falls gas station selling regular gas for $2.99 a gallon
local.summary: As drivers continue to feel a pinch at the pump, one Niagara Falls gas station is offering some relief: regular gasoline for just $2.99 a gallon.
local.body: As drivers continue to feel a pinch at the pump, one Niagara Falls gas station is offering some relief: regular gasoline for just $2.99 a gallon.SNK Fuels, located at 502 Main Street, was drawing plenty of attention on Thursday as drivers stopped to take advantage of the price."2.99 a gallon, you can't beat this," said customer Anthony Jones.The station is offering regular gasoline for $2.99 a gallon for customers paying with cash and $3.07 for credit customers.That's about $1.50 less per gallon than stations nearby and well below AAA's reported average of $4.18 a gallon for Niagara County.Zain Hussein, who owns the station, said the goal is to help people in the Niagara Falls community."We're not making any money, but we wanna do it for the people of Niagara Falls," Hussein said.Dusty Green, the station's manager, added Hussein is selling the gas at cost to give customers a break during a time when many families are struggling with expenses."Everyone's struggling right now, Christmas is coming up, the best thing he could possibly do is give back gas," Green said.WATCH: Niagara Falls gas station selling regular gas for $2.99 a gallonDrivers stopping at the station Thursday said the savings couldn't come at a better time, especially with the holidays approaching."2.99. I know it's insane. It's crazy," said Jeanette Garvis, who was visiting from New York City. "You don't find this price nowhere." Ronald Hinkle, of Buffalo, said he regularly drives between Lackawanna and Niagara Falls delivering the Challenger newspaper. The lower price means a little extra money stays in his pocket.Other customers echoed that sentiment"Trying to juggle housing, living situations and the gas prices, how high they were, this is a very big help," said Johniqua Mulkey of Niagara Falls.So how long will the $2.99 price last?Green said the gas will be available until the current supply sells out. When the station receives its next delivery, Hussein plans to offer that price again."I think everybody better come take advantage of these good gas prices, 2.99 a gallon," customer Anthony Jones said.

entertainment.title: Gilligan's Island Actor Dawn Wells' Final Role Was On A Show Based On A Popular Book Franchise
entertainment.summary: Before her passing in 2020, Gilligan's Island star Dawn Wells lent her voice to an animated series based on a popular children's book series.
entertainment.body:
The cartoon, which premiered on Netflix in 2018 but is now streaming on Peacock, is a spin-off of a 2017 DreamWorks Animation movie based on the popular children's book series by Dav Pilkey. More than 90 million copies of the books have sold worldwide.

Gumablina appears in a Season 3 episode that hit the streaming service in July 2019. "The Ghastly Danger of the Ghost Dentist" sees Wells' spectral tooth doctor haunt protagonists George and Harold after they tell a ghost story about her while camping with their friends. It turns out that Gumbalina isn't actually mean or scary, she's just really, really serious about oral hygiene, and when the boys allow her to clean everyone's teeth — Captain Underpants included — she leaves them alone.

The role was the final performance of Wells' before she died at 82 in 2020 due to complications from COVID-19. With her death, Ginger Grant actress Tina Louise became the last surviving member of the "Gilligan's Island" cast .

Netflix/YouTube Dawn Wells was 80 years old when she played Gumbalina Toothington in "The Epic Tales of Captain Underpants," and despite a long career with plenty of credits well beyond "Gilligan's Island," the part was somewhat unusual for her — and not just because she was playing a ghost dentist.

"Captain Underpants" was only Wells' second-ever voice acting credit. Her first? Reprising her role as Mary Ann Summers in the CBS Saturday morning cartoon series "Gilligan's Planet," which ran for one season in 1982. Notably, Tina Louise was the only member of the live-action cast not to return for the cartoon, so Wells pulled double duty on "Gilligan's Planet" and voiced Ginger Grant, too.

None of the "Gilligan's Island" castaways did much voice acting with one very notable exception — the great Jim Backus. In addition to his tenure as Thurston Howell III and many other live-action sitcom roles throughout his career, Backus voiced the comically nearsighted cartoon character Mr. Magoo for decades.
